content.text: Quality Assurance (QA) means the planned processes used to monitor, evaluate and improve the quality of the education a school provides. In Eduversal Partner Schools, quality assurance includes:

items: Evaluation: Judging how well teaching, learning, curriculum, assessment and operations work, based on evidence
Monitoring: Regular tracking of key performance indicators, student outcomes and how programs are carried out
Improvement: Actions to close the gaps that have been found, based on data and stakeholder feedback
Accountability: Open reporting to stakeholders about school performance and progress toward goals
content.title: 17.1.1 Definitions and Core Concepts

content.text: Eduversal's approach to quality assurance follows these principles:

steps: Student-Centered Focus: All quality assurance activities put the impact on student learning, wellbeing and development first
Evidence-Based Decision Making: Decisions are based on reliable data from several sources
Continuous Improvement Culture: QA is seen as a tool for development, not purely for evaluation
Stakeholder Engagement: Teachers, students, parents and community members help to evaluate quality
Alignment with Standards: QA processes match Cambridge International, CIS/WASC and Indonesian regulatory requirements
Transparency and Fairness: QA processes are explained clearly, applied the same way every time, and open to review
Action-Oriented: Findings lead to specific, measurable improvement actions, with clear responsibility for each action
content.title: 17.1.2 Principles of Effective Quality Assurance

content.text:
The Eduversal QA framework works at three connected levels:

Level 1: Classroom Level

items: Departmental moderation and standardization

content.text: The Eduversal Quality Management System brings together several evaluation tools and platforms. Together, they give a full picture of school performance. Key Components:

steps: EASE (Eduversal Analytical & Skills Evaluation): The umbrella assessment brand. EASE Growth is a curriculum-independent benchmark of Mathematical Reasoning, Science Literacy, and English Reading. EASE Assessment measures student achievement in Cambridge and National curriculum subjects through Teacher-Paced and Synchronized Tests. EASE Academic is the teacher subject-knowledge exam, used for professional development only
EduNav Platform: A digital quality management system with dashboards, KPI tracking and evidence storage
DTP (Development of Teaching Proficiency): A professional development program that helps teachers keep growing
Appraisal Program: Planned evaluation of teacher and school performance against set standards
School Improvement Plan (SIP): A strategic planning tool that links goals to actions and tracks progress
content.title: 17.2.1 Overview of the QMS

content.text: The QMS components work together to create a coherent improvement cycle: [Strategic Goals in SIP] ↓ [KPI Targets in EduNav] ↓ [Teaching Practice monitored through Appraisal Program] ↓ [Student Learning measured through EASE & Cambridge Assessments] ↓ [Professional Development via DTP based on identified needs] ↓ [Progress reviewed and SIP adjusted] ↓ [Cycle repeats]

subsections.title: Lesson Study and Professional Learning Communities (PLCs)

content.text:
Lesson study is a form of professional development in which teachers work together. They plan, observe, analyze and improve lessons together to make teaching more effective. Lesson Study Process:

Phase 1: Collaborative Planning (1-2 weeks)

items: Team identifies a learning goal or student challenge
Research best practices and choose teaching strategies
Write a detailed lesson plan that predicts how students will respond
Decide the observation focus and how to collect data
content.title: 17.4.1 Lesson Study Cycles

items: One team member teaches the lesson
Other team members observe using agreed protocols
Observers collect evidence on student thinking and engagement
Video recording may be used (with appropriate consent)
The teacher who taught the lesson reflects on it
Observers share evidence and insights
Team analyzes student learning outcomes
Identify what worked, what didn't, and why
Revise lesson based on insights
A different team member may teach the lesson again to another class
Further observation and analysis
Document learning for wider sharing
Team prepares summary of learning
Shares insights at department or whole-school meeting
Lesson plan and analysis added to EduNav resource library
Consider publishing or presenting at professional conferences
Each teacher participates in at least 2 lesson study cycles per year
Department time set aside for planning together
Principal and/or instructional coaches help run and support the cycles
Lesson study findings feed into department improvement plans

content.text: PLCs (Professional Learning Communities) are teams of educators who work together. They focus on the continuous improvement of teaching and student learning through inquiry and data analysis. PLC Structure and Function: Regular Meetings:

subsections.title: External Quality Assurance: Eduversal School Appraisal

content.text: The Eduversal School Appraisal is the network's external quality-assurance review of a partner school. It runs as an annual Phase 0-4 cycle with two on-site visits. Eduversal Subject Specialists carry it out, using the Eduversal School Appraisal Framework. It evaluates the school's performance across five domains:

steps: D1 — Leadership & Governance: vision and strategic direction, SMART goals and the P.I.E. model, leadership structure, performance management, governance and compliance
D2 — Teaching & Learning Quality: lesson planning and observation records, assessment methods, student goal-setting, feedback quality, evaluation of teaching, LMS and technology integration

D3 — Curriculum & Academic Programs: subject department structure, department meetings and HoD coordination, teacher self-assessment, formal observations and walkthroughs, mentoring and peer observation, PD evaluation, resources, digital policy

D4 — Student Achievement & Learning Outcomes: achievement data and dashboards, the Olympiad program and its wellbeing management, support for advanced students, language support, identification of and support for extra learning needs

D5 — School Culture & Community: culture, climate and student behavior, safeguarding and child protection, communication structures, co-curricular programs, parent and community engagement, staff wellbeing
content.title: 17.8.1 Purpose and Scope of School Appraisal

content.text: Phase 0 — Kickoff (online, in batches of 3-4 schools, about three weeks before that school's Phase 1 visit). The school receives the self-evaluation instructions and the School Appraisal: Evidence Guide 26-27. Completing or updating the Self-Evaluation Summary and working evidence links in the Evidence Guide is MANDATORY before each on-site visit. It is due at least five working days before the visit. If a school has not submitted it, the school's visit is rescheduled. The visit cannot go ahead without it.

items: The school rates itself on all 33 aspects across the five domains and attaches evidence to each
Evidence is kept in the school's own online storage. It is linked, aspect by aspect, in the Evidence Guide workbook. The workbook is sent to the Visit I Supervisor
Documents include: strategic plans, organizational charts, meeting minutes, student performance reports, policy documents, sample assessments
content.title: 17.8.2 School Appraisal Process

items: Completes self-evaluation against appraisal criteria
Identifies areas of strength and areas for development
Prepares questions, or names areas where the school wants guidance
Visit dates are confirmed with the school's Visit I and Visit II Supervisors
Stakeholder meetings are arranged (staff, students, parents/Board)
Facilities and resources are prepared for appraisal activities

content.text: Phase 1 — Teaching Quality Visit (on-site, 1-2 days): a team of five Subject Specialists attends, one per domain. The team always includes that school's Visit I Supervisor. Focus: classroom practice, teacher appraisal, curriculum implementation, assessment quality.

items: Formative lesson observations of teachers across subjects (Glow / Grow / Go feedback, no teacher score). Each observation uses two lenses at once: general teaching quality and subject-specific expertise
Rapid random classroom walkthroughs (10-15 minutes each) using the Teaching Practice Walkthrough. The Learner Experience Walkthrough is used alongside it (both formative, no individual teacher score)
Feedback sessions with observed teachers
Interviews with students and teachers, and per-domain meetings with school management

content.text: Phase 3 — Leadership, Technology & Facility Visit, the "Validation Visit" (on-site, 1-2 days, 55-63 days after Phase 1). Again a five-person team attends, one per domain. The team includes that school's Visit II Supervisor. The visit validates the school's self-appraisal and produces the Annual School Quality Report.

items: Review of the school's self-evaluation evidence against all five domains
Meetings with school leadership (Principal, Vice-Principals, Subject Leaders) and with AFT, Olympiad, project, club, after-school and college-counseling coordinators
Focus group discussions with teachers (3-4 participants)
Student focus groups (4-6 students from different year groups)
Review of facilities, resources, and operational systems
Rapid random walkthroughs as a spot-check that Phase 1 findings still hold

content.text: Post-Appraisal Meeting and oral exit report, at the end of each on-site visit:

items: Closing meeting with the Principal and leadership team
Appraisal team shares preliminary observations
Highlights commendations, recommendations, and concerns
A chance for the school to ask questions to clarify points

content.text: Annual School Quality Report (within 3 weeks of the Phase 3 Validation Visit). It is sent to the Eduversal Chief Academic Officer (CAO), the School Principal and the Academic Coordinator:

items: Summary of findings from the Phase 1 Teaching Quality Visit and the Phase 3 Validation Visit
Domain ratings across all five domains on the 1-4 scale, plus specific commendations (minimum 2) and priority recommendations (maximum 3)

Teacher Appraisal aggregate data and the EASE Academic participation rate, at school level and anonymized. EASE Academic scores are confidential to the teacher and are never reported into school appraisal. The report also gives the school's EASE Assessment performance summary and the EASE Growth Version 1 baseline summary, as context only (not scored)

A Development Rating for each of the five domains, banded as Outstanding (3.5-4.0) / Strong (2.5-3.4) / Developing (1.5-2.4) / Needs Intervention (1.0-1.4). Eduversal does not publish a single composite school score: the five domains measure different things, and a mean would hide the differences that matter for action. The rating is a development indicator, not a ranking. Schools are assessed against the framework standard, not against each other

content.text: School Response and Action Planning. Within two weeks of receiving the report, the school transfers its two School Development Priorities into the Appraisal Suite: School Development Plan 26-27. These are the two priorities agreed and recorded in the report. The response follows these steps:

items: Leadership team reviews report thoroughly
Develops action plan addressing recommendations
Assigns responsibilities, timelines, and resources
Submits action plan to Eduversal for review

content.text: Monitoring and Progress Reporting (ongoing). Each school is assigned two experts: a Visit I Supervisor and a Visit II Supervisor. Both come from the school's own visit teams, so both have attended. The Visit I Supervisor is the school's main point of contact through the year. The Visit I Supervisor writes and signs the Annual School Quality Report after Phase 3. This is the cycle’s single written report (Phases 0-2 produce none). The Visit II Supervisor leads the Phase 3 visit and provides cover. Supervisory load is balanced: each of the ten experts supervises exactly three schools.

items: The school updates its action plan progress in Academic Hub

Phase 2 Progress Check-in (online, 1-2 hours), led by the Visit I Supervisor. It takes place at the midpoint between Phase 1 and Phase 3. It covers self-appraisal progress across all five domains, action plan implementation status and emerging concerns
Supervisors log Coordinator Notes at any point in the year. Supervisors escalate to the CAO when a school's outcome status changes to Needs Support or Critical Attention
Follow-up Sessions (online or on-site) are triggered by outcome status or by a Coordinator Note escalation, not by the calendar

Phase 4 Impact Review (online, near the end of the academic year), led by the Visit I Supervisor with an Eduversal representative. Each of the two School Development Priorities receives an impact status. This is recorded in an Impact Review Record. The Impact Review creates no new Domain Rating

content.text:
Eduversal Partner Schools use the PDSA cycle as a framework for continuous improvement at all levels:

Plan:

items: Identify a problem or opportunity for improvement
Analyze root causes using data and stakeholder input
Develop a hypothesis: "If we do X, then Y will improve because Z"
Design a small-scale pilot or intervention
Set success criteria and decide how to collect data
content.title: 17.9.1 Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) Methodology

items: Carry out the pilot on a small scale (e.g., one class, one grade level)
Collect data systematically during implementation
Record what happens, including unexpected results
Analyze the data collected
Compare results to predictions and success criteria
Identify what worked, what didn't, and why
Consider contextual factors influencing outcomes

items.text: Decide on next steps based on findings:
items: Adopt: Use the successful intervention across the whole school
Adapt: Change the intervention and repeat the cycle
Abandon: Stop the unsuccessful approach and try a different strategy
Communicate learning to stakeholders
Update policies, practices or the SIP where needed

content.text:
Example 1: Improving EAL Student Writing Outcomes

Plan:

items: Problem: EAL students in Year 7 score below target on writing assessments
Root cause analysis: Limited academic vocabulary and sentence structure skills
Hypothesis: If we run daily 10-minute activities that build academic vocabulary, EAL students' writing scores will improve
Pilot: One Year 7 class for one term
Success criteria: 20% improvement in writing assessment scores; teacher observation of increased vocabulary use
content.title: 17.9.2 PDSA Examples in School Context

items: Use the daily vocabulary routine in the pilot class
Collect weekly vocabulary assessments and writing samples
Document teacher observations
End-of-term data shows 25% improvement in pilot class
Non-pilot EAL classes improved only 5%
The teacher notes that students are more confident using academic language
Adopt: Extend the academic vocabulary routine to all Year 7 classes
Adapt: Create subject-specific vocabulary lists for different departments
Share findings at PLC meeting
Include vocabulary development in the English department improvement plan

content.text:
Example 2: Reducing Behavior Incidents During Lunch

Plan:

items: Problem: More behavior incidents during the lunch period
Root cause analysis: Not enough supervision and few structured activities
Hypothesis: If we add structured activities and have more supervisors present, incidents will fall by 50%
Pilot: A one-week trial with the new schedule and activities
Success criteria: 50% reduction in incident reports; improved student satisfaction
Implement extra supervision roster
Organize structured games and activities
Collect incident reports and carry out a student survey
Incidents fell by 60% during the pilot week
Student survey shows high satisfaction with new activities
Some practical problems with scheduling supervisors
Adopt: Continue the structured lunch activities and the stronger supervision
Adapt: Change the supervisor schedule for better coverage
Share the positive results with parents and the Board
Write the new procedures into the Student Behavior Management policy
Every improvement action is logged with a unique ID
Fields include: action description, rationale, responsible person, timeline, success criteria, status updates
Each action is linked to the relevant SIP goal and evidence documents

Progress updates are required at set intervals

content.text:
The SSER (Section 17.7) is the base for the self-study required for CIS/WASC accreditation:

Connection Between SSER and Self-Study:

items: The annual SSER builds up evidence and analysis over several years
The self-study is a deeper, fuller version of the SSER, aligned to the accreditation protocol
A habit of annual self-evaluation makes the full self-study less difficult
Evidence collected for the SSER is ready to use for the self-study
content.title: 17.14.2 Self-Study Process

items: 12-18 months before the accreditation visit, the school starts the formal self-study process
A self-study committee is formed with representatives from all stakeholder groups
SSER and QA data from the previous 3-5 years are collected and analyzed
Writing tasks are assigned for each standard/category
Stakeholder surveys and focus groups are carried out
The draft self-study is shared for feedback and then revised
All evidence is indexed and stored in EduNav so it is easy to find
Physical and digital evidence rooms are prepared
Key documents bookmarked and highlighted
Staff are told where to find evidence and how to talk about their work
content.title: 17.14.3 Accreditation Visit Preparation

items: Staff, students and parents are told about the accreditation process and visit schedule
Key messages about the school's strengths and improvement work are shared
An honest picture of the school is encouraged - no "window dressing" (making things look better than they are)
The visit schedule is planned together with the visiting team
Facilities prepared (workspace, technology, refreshments)
Transportation and accommodation are arranged if needed
Visiting team report reviewed thoroughly
Commendations celebrated and publicized
Recommendations addressed in action plan
Progress on recommendations is monitored and reported
Evidence of how the school responded is included in the next cycle
Crosswalk document that maps handbook sections to CIS/WASC standards
Evidence index showing where each artifact is kept and how often it is updated

Draft and final self-study documents

content.text: Quality assurance and internal review are not goals in themselves. They are ways to reach the main goal: better student learning, development and wellbeing. A good QA system is:

items: Comprehensive: Covers every part of school operations, from classroom teaching to financial management
Systematic: Follows regular cycles and protocols; it does not just react to events as they happen
Evidence-Based: Uses reliable data from several sources, not guesses or stories
Collaborative: Involves all stakeholders in the evaluation and improvement process
Action-Oriented: Uses findings to make specific improvements, not just to produce reports
Sustainable: Part of school culture and routines, and does not depend on individual leaders

content.text: The Principal's leadership is key to building and keeping this QA culture. The Principal models reflective practice and celebrates learning. The Principal also makes it psychologically safe to evaluate honestly, and makes sure that QA findings lead to real action. In this way, the Principal sets the tone for continuous improvement across the school. When quality assurance is done well, it becomes a strong tool for professional learning and strategic decision-making. In the end, it leads to better outcomes for students. It gives the evidence for celebrating successes and the insights for dealing with challenges. It also gives the roadmap for ongoing growth as an educational institution.
